newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Truth body stirs hornet's nest in S.African press.
newsitem.headline: Truth body stirs hornet's nest in S.African press.

text.p: South Africa's official reconciliation initiative was under fire on Wednesday from black journalists over the way it plans to probe white-run media during the apartheid era.

A statement from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, said it would review its inquiry into the media following a two-hour meeting on Tuesday night with members of the Black Editors' Forum and the Forum of Black Journalists.

"We have to rethink our approach if important stakeholders find it impossible to participate," said the statement from Tutu's white deputy Alex Boraine, indicating an apparent boycott threat from the black journalists.
The truth commission is facing its own internal race problems, with senior black officials complaining that white liberals are getting key jobs.

Last year the commission asked the Freedom of Expression Institute (FXI) to prepare a report for it on media coverage during the apartheid years, when newspapers faced draconian curbs on what they could say.
"The commission is to review the mandate it has given to the FXI in preparations for hearings," the commission statement said.

The FXI research is directed by Raymond Louw, white former editor of the Rand Daily Mail, which took a vociferous anti-government stance during the apartheid years, before it was closed by its owners, purportedly on financial grounds.
But Thami Mazwai, head of the Black Editors' Forum, said Louw should not be involved in any inquiry because he had been part of a system that discriminated against black journalists.

Mazwai said the two companies that dominated press ownership through four decades of apartheid -- The Argus Group, now Independent Newspaper Holdings and South African Associated Newspapers, now Times Media Ltd -- "hardly raised a sweat in opposition to the then government's stranglehold on the media".

Mazwai and others say that papers like the Rand Daily Mail, despite their anti-apartheid image, imposed unnecessary self- censorship at the behest of their owners. The white-led government had powers to close newspapers which breached laws restricting coverage of security force action.
"Even when the state was implementing its various restrictive laws, there was very little opposition from the English media," Mazwai said.

Louw said the objections of black editors to the FXI compiling a report for the truth commission were misplaced because the report would be only one submission among many. Individual black journalists would be able to address the commission directly.
